reading.rtitle: The Last Weeks Before the Interview
paras: In the last weeks before an admissions interview, most candidates want to learn something new: one more structure, one more list of words. In my experience that is the wrong moment for it. The last weeks are for taking stock. I ask every candidate to record ten minutes of interview answers, and then we look at what is really there, not at what was studied.

With advanced speakers the recording almost always shows the same thing. Fluency is good, sometimes very good. But under pressure, they fall back on the three or four structures they trust, and the rest of what they know stays on the page. They are not getting worse. They are on a plateau, and the plateau is comfortable, because the structures they use never fail. That comfort zone is exactly the problem.

So I do not add anything. We choose two tools that the candidate already knows but avoids, and we fine-tune them until they are second nature. Every practice answer has to include one of them, even if it costs a few mistakes in accuracy. Candidates who do this rarely sound perfect in the interview. They sound like people who are still learning, and for a panel that is choosing students, that is the point.

listenings.text: The learners I worry about least are the ones who come to me and say they have stopped improving. That sentence tells me they are paying attention. The plateau is visible to them, so we can work on it. The ones I worry about are the ones who have not noticed. With advanced learners I see the same thing again and again. They understand almost everything, and their reading is excellent. But under pressure, in a meeting or in an interview, they fall back on the three or four structures they trust, and the others never leave the page. So I ask them for one thing, and only one. In every conversation, use one structure you are not completely sure of. It will cost you a few mistakes. That is the price of leaving your comfort zone, and it is the only price that has ever bought anybody any progress.

I run an engineering department, and I have worked in English for most of my career without ever being a native speaker, so I had to find a way to measure it. What I do is simple. Once a month I record five minutes of myself talking about my projects. Always without notes, always five minutes. Then I wait a week. You should never listen on the same day, because on the same day you hear what you meant to say. A week later you hear what you actually said, and that is a very different thing. When I started, the first change was fluency: fewer pauses, fewer restarts. Accuracy followed about six months later, almost by itself, because once you stop fighting for every sentence, you have the attention left over to get it right.
